subject: history
title: Interpreting Protest Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll judge sources and weigh how change came in Britain — from below, from above, or both?
meta_desc: GCSE History — interpretations of protest, reform and rights in Britain c.1170-present.
final_note: You weighed top-down reform against bottom-up protest as drivers of change in British rights.

concepts.def: 1688 overthrow of James II — secured parliamentary rule
1819 massacre of reform protesters in Manchester
Protest by smashing, marching or hunger strike
1807 trade abolished, 1833 slavery ended in Empire
Gay rights, race relations — won by 20th-c campaigns

walkthroughs.body_html:
Some argue change came when elites chose to give it.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688, the 1807 abolition of the slave trade, and the 1832 Great Reform Act were all passed by Parliament and the rich — not by mass revolt.

Others argue pressure from below mattered most.

The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 shocked elites. Peterloo in 1819 became a martyrdom. Chartists, unions and Suffragettes built mass campaigns that scared governments into reform.

From Magna Carta (1215) to the Equal Franchise Act (1928), rights expanded.

20th-century campaigns won race relations laws (1965, 1976) and gay rights (decriminalised in England 1967). Most historians see both push from below and concession from above at work.

mcqs.q: In what year did the Peterloo Massacre happen in Manchester?
In what year was the slave trade abolished in the British Empire?
What did Magna Carta actually do in 1215?
options: Magna Carta abolished the monarchy and created Parliament.
Magna Carta gave ordinary English people democratic rights and freedom.
Emmeline Pankhurst was the first woman to be elected Prime Minister.
It was a peace treaty between King John and rebel barons protecting baronial privileges and limiting arbitrary royal taxation and imprisonment — it was annulled within months.

mcqs.q: What did the 1832 Great Reform Act actually do?
options: The 1832 Reform Act allowed women to vote for the first time.
Magna Carta abolished the monarchy and created Parliament.
It abolished rotten boroughs, redistributed seats to industrial towns, and extended the vote to about 1 in 5 adult men — still far short of democracy.
The 1832 Reform Act gave the vote to all working men.

mcqs.q: Did suffragette militancy help or hinder votes for women?
options: Historians disagree — militancy raised the issue's profile but also alienated MPs; the suspension of activism in WWI may have done more to enable 1918 reform.
Emmeline Pankhurst was the first woman to be elected Prime Minister.
Suffragette militancy is the main reason women got the vote in 1918.
The 1832 Reform Act allowed women to vote for the first time.
